text: Stavros' hard constraint for the managed-volumes work: losing user data is unacceptable under any circumstance, no exceptions. This is why the volume code only ever deletes Docker's volume *records* (bookkeeping) and never volume contents, why ownership is proven by our own com.harbormaster.app label rather than inferred from a volume's shape, and why any Docker failure during stale-app cleanup skips that app's filesystem work rather than pressing on. When touching this area, prefer refusing to act over acting on an uncertain inference.

Rejected for managed volumes: emitting the volume definitions into a separate Compose override file passed with an extra -f, instead of rewriting the app's own Compose file. It is cleaner code and sidesteps YAML rewriting entirely, but Stavros wants the checked-out Compose file to stay self-contained so that a plain 'docker compose logs' or 'docker compose up' in the repo directory behaves identically to what Harbormaster runs. Avoiding that awkwardness was the original motivation for the whole feature (the  approach forces you to set environment variables before any manual Compose command), so an override file would have reintroduced the problem in a new form. Also rejected: persisting per-app state recording which apps ever enabled manage_volumes, proposed so stale-app cleanup could skip Docker entirely for legacy apps. Judged unnecessary complexity; the failure type is enough to decide.

The gitchangelog pre-commit hook was removed rather than repaired, and it should not be re-added in that shape. Two reasons, neither reconstructable now that the config is deleted. First, the entry was 'bash -c "gitchangelog > CHANGELOG.md"', so the shell truncated CHANGELOG.md before gitchangelog even started; when gitchangelog failed the file was left at zero bytes, and it destroyed an unreleased changelog entry once. Second, it ran at commit stage, where the commit being made is not yet in git history, so the file it wrote was permanently one commit behind. Fixing it via additional_dependencies was considered and does not work either: the hook was 'language: system', for which pre-commit ignores additional_dependencies. CHANGELOG.md is now maintained by hand between releases. UPDATE 2026-08-15: .gitchangelog.rc has since been deleted too. It had been kept only for the GitLab release job, which generated a changelog independently from PyPI, and that whole pipeline went away when the project moved to GitHub. Nothing reads gitchangelog config any more.

Stavros intends to adopt release-please for changelog and release management eventually (stated 2026-08-14, when the gitchangelog pre-commit hook was removed). This has not been done and there is no ticket for it yet. If changelog automation comes up again, prefer moving to release-please over reviving gitchangelog.

The mypy pre-commit hook needs 'attrs' in its additional_dependencies, not just type stubs. attrs is PEP 561 typed and has no separate stub package, and mypy's bundled attrs plugin cannot generate __init__ for the @attr.s classes unless it can resolve the import. Combined with --ignore-missing-imports, a missing attrs produced 15 misleading 'Unexpected keyword argument' errors on Paths, AppPaths and Configuration, with notes pointing at typeshed builtins.pyi because mypy had fallen back to type.__call__. If those errors reappear, suspect the hook environment, not the classes; the classes have never been wrong. This cost real diagnosis time once.

Stavros moved the project to GitHub and had the GitLab pipeline deleted (stated 2026-08-15). The GitHub Actions workflow now runs pre-commit and pytest and publishes Docker Hub images for pushes to master and v* release tags. The PyPI release job and the standalone Linux binary jobs (build image for linux build + build linux) were deliberately not ported; they remain manual and unautomated until someone wants them back. .gitchangelog.rc was deleted at the same time, as the GitLab release job was its last reader. UPDATE 2026-08-15: partly superseded. PyPI publishing is automated again, and images are no longer published from master pushes. See entry jrhqze. The standalone Linux binary jobs are still unported and still manual.

Rejected when the Python floor moved to 3.9 (2026-08-15): refreshing poetry.lock with 'poetry lock --regenerate'. It is the obvious response to 'pyproject.toml changed significantly since poetry.lock was last generated', and it does make CI pass on newer interpreters, but it bumps every dependency, including ruamel.yaml 0.17 to 0.19. ruamel.yaml is what the managed-volumes code uses to rewrite users' Compose files, an area under a hard no-data-loss constraint and the least battle-tested code in the project, so it must not ride along in an unrelated chore. A plain 'poetry lock' was enough: Poetry 2.x keeps locked versions by default, and the only change was dropping pytz, a 3.8-only transitive dependency. A real dependency refresh is still wanted and should be its own ticket with its own review.

Empirical, and not visible from the code: the locked ruamel-yaml-clib 0.2.8 is what caps CI's interpreter. On 3.13 it cannot install at all, as there is no wheel and the C extension fails to compile ('too few arguments to function _PyLong_AsByteArray'). On 3.11 and 3.12 the manylinux wheels install but are themselves malformed upstream, with the extension module at the wheel root instead of under ruamel/yaml/clib/, so 'from ruamel.yaml.clib import _ruamel_yaml' fails and ruamel.yaml silently runs in pure-Python mode. On 3.14 install succeeds only because ruamel.yaml stops requiring the clib there. So the C speedup has never actually been in use, and 3.14 passing is an accident of a dependency marker rather than evidence of support. CI is pinned to 3.12 on purpose.

Evidence gathered 2026-08-15, when dependencies were refreshed, for the deferred decision about raising the floor past 3.9. Re-resolving the lock with a temporary >=3.10 floor showed these packages are held back purely by 3.9: click 8.1.8 wants 8.4.2, pytest 8.4.2 wants 9.1.1, Sphinx 7.4.7 wants 8.1.3, myst-parser 3.0.1 wants 4.0.1, sphinxcontrib-mermaid 1.2.3 wants 2.1.0, requests, urllib3, alabaster, iniconfig, linkify-it-py, mdit-py-plugins and uc-micro-py all want newer, and importlib-metadata plus zipp would stop being needed at all. The newest myst-parser and Sphinx need something newer still. Nothing here is urgent, and click is the one that matters, as it is a runtime dependency rather than a docs one. Stavros deliberately deferred the floor decision as a separate judgement about the user base.

Rejected while adding Compose filename discovery (compose.yaml/compose.yml/docker-compose.yaml/docker-compose.yml): automatically picking up Compose's override files (compose.override.yaml and friends) alongside the discovered file, and discovering more than one file in general. Discovery resolves to exactly one file; a multi-file stack still needs an explicit compose_config listing every file in merge order. The reason is that Harbormaster already has an explicit multi-file mechanism, and silently appending an override file would make the set of files Harbormaster runs differ from what the user declared, for a case nobody has asked for. Revisit only if someone actually hits it.

Harbormaster adopted release-please (2026-08-15), completing the intent recorded earlier. Three decisions from Stavros that are not deducible from the config files. First, the Docker Hub :latest tag now means 'last release', not 'last master build'. It previously tracked master, so this is a deliberate behaviour change for anyone pulling :latest. Second, PyPI publishing is automated via OIDC trusted publishing rather than an API token, so there is no PyPI secret in the repo; the trust relationship is configured on pypi.org and will silently break if the workflow filename changes. Third, versioning deliberately mirrors skorokithakis/catt: bump-patch-for-minor-pre-major and bump-minor-pre-major are both true, so while below 1.0.0 a feat: commit bumps patch, not minor. Stavros confirmed he wants patch. A PAT (as catt uses via RELEASE_PLEASE_TOKEN) was considered and rejected here: catt needs one only because its publish workflow triggers on tag pushes, which GITHUB_TOKEN-created tags cannot fire. Harbormaster instead runs the publish jobs inside the release-please workflow gated on its outputs, so plain GITHUB_TOKEN suffices and there is no token to rotate.

Two GitHub traps hit while getting Harbormaster's first release-please release (v0.3.5) out, both invisible in the code and both costing an hour. First: a repository ruleset named 'Version' targeting refs/tags/v* had a 'creation' rule, which blocked release-please from creating the tag. Stavros removed the creation rule (2026-08-15), keeping deletion, non_fast_forward and update, so release tags are still immutable once made. Do not re-add 'creation': GitHub Actions cannot be granted a bypass on a personal repo's ruleset, the API rejects it with 'Actor GitHub Actions integration must be part of the ruleset source or owner organization', so a creation rule and automated releases are mutually exclusive here. Second, and much more obscure: creating a GitHub Release whose target commit adds or modifies anything under .github/workflows/ relative to the default branch requires the 'workflows: write' permission, which GITHUB_TOKEN can never hold, and the API reports this as a bare 403 'Resource not accessible by integration' rather than naming the permission. Release-please targets the release PR's merge commit, so this never fires in the normal flow. It fired here because the first release attempt failed on the ruleset and a workflow file was then changed before retrying, which left the merge commit permanently unreleasable. The fix was to revert the workflow change so the trees matched again. Rule of thumb: when a release is stuck, land it before touching any workflow file. A GitHub App installation token would avoid both traps, and was considered and rejected as not worth the maintenance.
